title: First commandment (CCC 2084–2141)
hook: faith, hope and love of God, and no superstition

segments.voice: Yesterday, the precepts: five basic duties, a floor and not a ceiling. Your line was the minimum, not the maximum. Which one did you stretch a little? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-four.

A phone lights up at 7 a.m. with a daily horoscope: avoid big decisions, the stars are not on your side. On the dashboard, a little charm swings from the mirror. In a drawer, the lucky socks from the playoff game. None of it looks like religion. Maybe a joke, maybe a half-belief. Today the Catechism starts walking through the commandments, one at a time, and it begins with the commandment that has something to say about all of that, and about a great deal more.
screen: `A HOROSCOPE AT 7 A.M.` → `A CHARM ON THE MIRROR.` → `THE LUCKY SOCKS.`

segments.voice: In Exodus, the commandments open with God speaking first about what he has done, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the Lord thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage." Only then comes the command: "Thou shalt not have strange gods before me." Rescue first, then the rule. The Catechism reads this commandment as a call to the three great virtues aimed straight at God. Faith: trusting God and what he has revealed. Hope: expecting from him, confidently, the help to love him and to reach the life he promises. Charity: loving God above everything, for his own sake. When Jesus is tempted in the desert, he answers with words the Catechism places under this commandment, in the Douay-Rheims: "The Lord thy God shalt thou adore, and him only shalt thou serve." Adoration, prayer, sacrifice, keeping promises made to God: the Catechism names them all as ways of putting God first. Then it names what pushes God out of first place. Idolatry: making a god of anything that isn't God, which the Catechism says can be power, pleasure, race, ancestors, the state, money. Divination: horoscopes, astrology, palm reading, consulting mediums, all trying to grab hold of the future instead of trusting it to God. And superstition, which the Catechism describes in a careful way: not only lucky charms, but treating even good religious practices as if they worked like magic, by their outward form alone. A medal, a novena, a candle are not the problem. Thinking they force God's hand is. So in this reading the first commandment isn't mostly a ban. It's a question of order: whatever sits in first place in a life is what that life serves.
screen: `RESCUE FIRST, THEN THE RULE.` · `FAITH, HOPE AND LOVE OF GOD.` · `IDOLATRY AND DIVINATION.` · `SUPERSTITION: GOOD THINGS USED AS MAGIC.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drop one superstition. Settle, and breathe. If there is one, let a small habit come to mind that you lean on for luck: a ritual before a game, a number you avoid, a horoscope you check, a chain message you forward just in case. Look at it plainly. Ask what it's really asking for: safety, control, a good outcome. If you pray, you can hand that same wish to God directly. If you don't, just notice the wish underneath the habit, and decide, for today, to set the habit down. The bell holds the time.
First commandment. Thou shalt not have strange gods before me: faith, hope and love aimed at God first, and no idol, fortune-telling or superstition in his place. Today's word.
Your line: god first. Today, when you catch yourself reaching for a bit of luck, pause, and put first things first. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics learn the commandments in catechism and use them in an examination of conscience before confession; the first is kept through prayer, the Mass, and trusting God over luck and fortune-telling.

fork.reveal: in Matthew 4 Jesus answers with the words the Catechism places under the first commandment: God alone is adored.

notes: CCC 2084–2141 paraphrased (copyrighted translation). Faith/hope/charity (2087–2094), idolatry (2112–2114), divination (2115–2117), superstition (2111).

Numbering of the commandments differs between churches (Catholic numbering follows Augustine); not raised in the lesson.
